title: The Hidden Rabies Risk in Vietnam's Unregulated Dog Meat Trade
excerpt: Informal slaughter practices create direct exposure pathways for rabies and other zoonotic diseases. Without regulated facilities, the risk to workers and consumers remains unquantified and unmanaged.
body_html:
Vietnam's dog meat trade operates entirely outside the formal food safety system. There are zero registered slaughterhouses — meaning no inspections, no safety protocols, and no disease screening at any point in the supply chain.

Rabies is the most acute risk. Dogs transported long distances under extreme stress show suppressed immune responses, and informal slaughter conditions — often involving blunt force — create direct blood and saliva exposure for workers and bystanders. The Ho Chi Minh City Food Safety Management Authority has issued multiple consumption warnings in recent years, citing these exact pathways.

E. coli and Salmonella contamination are also endemic in unregulated meat handling environments. Without refrigeration, sanitation, or inspection, contamination rates in informal dog meat markets are significantly higher than in regulated meat sectors.

This is not a marginal issue. With an estimated 5 million dogs entering the trade annually, the scale of unregulated meat handling represents a genuine and ongoing public health risk — one that receives far less attention than it deserves.

95% of Vietnamese respondents support ending this trade — and the public health argument is one of the strongest reasons why. Sign the petition to demand regulated food safety standards and a permanent ban.
author: AI Research Team

title: Stolen in the Night: How Pet Theft Feeds the Dog Meat Supply Chain
excerpt: Organised theft networks target family pets in both rural and urban Vietnam, transporting them hundreds of kilometres to informal markets. Many victims are beloved companions stolen from their homes.
body_html:
The dog meat supply chain in Vietnam runs significantly on stolen pets. Organised theft networks — some operating across multiple provinces — target family dogs in both rural villages and urban neighbourhoods, using poison bait, traps, and motorbike-mounted wire snares to capture animals quickly and quietly.

Dogs are crammed into wire mesh cages, often 10–20 animals per cage, without food, water, or veterinary care. They are then transported hundreds of kilometres to informal markets or directly to unlicensed slaughter points. By the time they arrive, many are severely dehydrated or injured.

For the families they were taken from, the loss is devastating. Dogs in Vietnam are not livestock — they are companions, protectors, and family members. The cultural and emotional bond between Vietnamese families and their dogs is precisely what makes this trade so deeply opposed by the public.

A 2021 survey found that 95% of Vietnamese respondents support ending the trade — a number that reflects widespread moral rejection, not fringe advocacy. The theft of family pets is cited as one of the top reasons for this overwhelming public consensus.

No registered slaughterhouse exists anywhere in Vietnam. This trade operates entirely in the shadows — and it thrives there. Sign the petition to demand accountability and a permanent ban.
author: AI Research Team

title: 95% of Vietnamese Want the Trade to End. So Why Hasn't It?
excerpt: A 2021 survey found overwhelming public support for ending the dog meat trade in Vietnam. The barriers are political and economic — not cultural. Here's what's standing in the way.
body_html:
The data is unambiguous: 95% of Vietnamese respondents in a 2021 survey support ending the dog meat trade, explicitly rejecting the idea that it is a cultural necessity. This is not a fringe position — it is a supermajority mandate.

So why does the trade persist? The barriers are structural, not cultural. A small number of economic actors — traders, transport operators, and informal slaughter operators — have an active financial interest in maintaining the status quo. Without formal regulation, there is no mechanism to enforce a ban even if one were enacted tomorrow.

Political momentum has been slow. Local governments in Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City have issued advisory recommendations to reduce dog meat consumption, citing public health risks and international scrutiny. But advisory recommendations are not law, and enforcement is non-existent.

The path to change runs through the Communist Party of Vietnam and food safety authorities — the bodies with actual regulatory power. A sustained, locally-led campaign applying public pressure through formal petition channels is the most effective lever available.

This campaign exists to be that lever. Sign the petition and join the 95% who are already on the right side of this issue.
author: AI Research Team

title: No Slaughterhouses, No Oversight: The Full Scale of Vietnam's Food Safety Gap
excerpt: The complete absence of registered dog meat slaughterhouses creates an untracked, uninspected supply chain operating in plain sight — and what it would take to change that.
body_html:
In every formal food sector in Vietnam, there is a regulatory baseline: registered facilities, inspection regimes, sanitation standards. The dog meat trade has none of these. There is not a single registered dog meat slaughterhouse in Vietnam — a fact confirmed by food safety authorities in Ho Chi Minh City.

This creates a food safety gap with no equivalent in the formal meat sector. Animals enter the supply chain with no health screening. Slaughter occurs in uncontrolled environments. Meat is handled and distributed without cold chain management or pathogen testing. Consumers have no way to assess the safety of what they are consuming.

The comparison to countries that have enacted bans is instructive. The Philippines banned the dog meat trade in 1998 under the Animal Welfare Act, and South Korea has been progressively restricting it through legislation. In both cases, the regulatory argument — food safety, public health, disease control — was as central as animal welfare in driving legislative change.

Vietnam has the public mandate to act. 95% of Vietnamese respondents support ending this trade. What is missing is political will and formal enforcement mechanisms. A petition directed at the Communist Party and food safety authorities is the most direct way to close that gap.

Add your signature and demand the regulatory oversight that protects public health.
author: AI Research Team

title: Lucky: The Dog Who Became the Face of a Movement
excerpt: For nine years, Lucky has been a priceless member of his Vietnamese family. His story — and why his owners decided they could no longer stay silent about the trade threatening dogs like him.
body_html:
Lucky is a purebred Vietnamese Ta dog — nine years old, with the quiet dignity of an animal who has spent his whole life as a treasured family companion. To his owners, he is not a pet in the casual sense. He is a presence in the home, a protector, a source of daily joy. He has a name. He has a history. He is, as his family says, a priceless treasure.

Lucky's story is the reason this campaign exists. Not because his situation is unique — but because it isn't. Across Vietnam, millions of dogs just like Lucky live in exactly this kind of bond with their families. And millions of them are at risk from a trade their owners never consented to.

Pet theft is rampant. Organised networks target dogs in both rural and urban areas. A dog like Lucky — healthy, well-fed, clearly cared for — is exactly the kind of target these networks seek out. The moment he leaves the garden, the risk becomes real.

Lucky's owners decided they could not stay silent. They knew that 95% of Vietnamese people share their values — that dogs are family members, not food — and that this shared belief is the foundation on which lasting change can be built.

This campaign is their voice, and the voice of every Vietnamese family that has lost a pet, or lives in fear of losing one. Sign the petition and stand with them.
author: Campaign Team
